entry: American former [[Basketball|basketball]] player who spent 21 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association (NBA)]], mainly with the Minnesota Timberwolves and [[Boston Celtics]]. Drafted fifth overall out of high school in 1995, he won the NBA Most Valuable Player Award in 2004 and was named Defensive Player of the Year for the 2007–08 season, when he helped the Celtics reach the 2008 NBA Finals, where they beat the [[Los Angeles Lakers]]. He was named to 15 All-Star Games and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2020.

American comedian and actor. Hart broke through when Judd Apatow cast him in the TV series *Undeclared* (2001). His first stand-up album, *I'm a Grown Little Man* (2009), was followed by four more comedy albums. His films include *Scary Movie 3* (2003), *Think Like a Man* (2012), *Ride Along* (2014) and the *Jumanji* franchise. In 2017 he launched the Laugh Out Loud Network, a streaming service, in partnership with Lionsgate. He received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor in 2024, and [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him to its list of the 100 most influential people in 2015.

English football player and manager who played as an attacking midfielder or forward. He was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979 while playing for Hamburger SV. At [[Liverpool]] he had won three First Division titles, two [[UEFA]] Cups, the FA Cup and the European Cup. He earned 63 caps for England, scoring 21 goals and captaining the team 31 times. As a manager he won promotion to the [[Premier League]] with Newcastle United, and in October 2000 he resigned as England manager after a 1–0 loss to Germany in qualification for the 2002 FIFA World Cup.

American stage and screen actor. Kline began his career on stage in 1972 with The Acting Company and won three Tony Awards, the most recent for Best Actor in a Play in 2017. He made his film debut in *Sophie's Choice* (1982) opposite [[Meryl Streep]] and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *A Fish Called Wanda* (1988). His other films include *The Big Chill* (1983), *Dave* (1993) and *Beauty and the Beast* (2017). Since 2011 he has voiced Calvin Fischoeder in the animated [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *Bob's Burgers*.

American stage and screen actor. He won two [[Academy Awards]], for Best Supporting Actor in *The Usual Suspects* (1995) and Best Actor in *American Beauty* (1999). He starred as Frank Underwood in the [[Netflix]] series *House of Cards* (2013–2017), which won him a Golden Globe Award. From 2004 to 2015 he was artistic director of the Old Vic in London. Beginning in 2017 he faced allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denied. In 2018 and 2019 he faced criminal investigations, but he was either not charged or the charges were dropped. In 2023 a London jury acquitted him of [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]] charges.

Strong, heat-resistant synthetic aramid fiber related to Nomex. Developed by Stephanie Kwolek at [[DuPont]] in 1965, Kevlar was first used commercially in the early 1970s as a replacement for steel in racing tires. Its high tensile strength-to-weight ratio makes it five times stronger than steel by this measure, and it is used in [[Bulletproof vest|bulletproof vests]], bicycle tires, racing sails and mooring lines. It is spun into ropes or fabric, or used as an ingredient in [[Composite material|composite]] components. A similar fiber, Twaron, was developed by Akzo in the 1970s.

[[Musical instrument]] played using a keyboard, a row of levers pressed by the fingers. The most common are the [[Piano|piano]], [[Pipe organ|organ]] and electronic keyboards, including [[Synthesizer|synthesizers]] and digital pianos. The term classifies instruments by how they are played rather than how their sound is produced, grouping them into families such as aerophones, including the pipe organ and [[Accordion|accordion]], and chordophones, including the [[Harpsichord|harpsichord]] and clavichord. In musicology, the term can also mean an instrument of uncertain identity, since the harpsichord, clavichord and early piano competed in the 18th century. The earliest known keyboard instrument was the ancient Greek *hydraulis*, a pipe organ invented in the third century BC. The first template for the modern piano was introduced in 1698 by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Italy.

Russian former [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial artist]] who competed in the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship]] (UFC) lightweight division. He held the UFC lightweight title from April 2018 to March 2021, the longest reign of any champion in the division, and retired with 29 wins and no losses. After his victory over [[Conor McGregor]] at UFC 229, he attacked McGregor's teammates, and the Nevada State Athletic Commission fined him $500,000 and suspended him for nine months. Trained in [[Wrestling|wrestling]] and [[Judo|judo]], he was inducted into the UFC Hall of Fame in 2022.

First wife of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]. Khadija was a wealthy merchant from an aristocratic clan of the Quraysh, admired for her integrity and business success. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to [[Syria]] and later offered him marriage. They had six children, including [[Fatima]]. After Muhammad's first revelation, Khadija is credited as the first convert to Islam, and she supported him throughout her life. [[Muslims]] honor her as Mother of the Believers, and her grave in [[Mecca]] attracts many pilgrims. She is also counted among the Four Ladies of Heaven, alongside Fatima, Asiya and Mary, mother of Jesus.

Kuwaiti-born Pakistani militant and former head of propaganda for [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]]. The 9/11 Commission called him "the principal architect" of the [[September 11 attacks]]. He was captured in [[Rawalpindi]] in 2003 in a joint operation by the [[Central Intelligence Agency|CIA]] and Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence, and he has been held at Guantanamo Bay since 2006. In 2024 he agreed to plead guilty in exchange for a life sentence, but the deal was revoked by Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin and voided by a D.C. appeals court in 2025. Critics argue that his admissions, obtained through torture, are inadmissible.

Arab Muslim commander who served the prophet [[Muhammad]] and the Rashidun caliphs [[Abu Bakr]] and [[Umar]]. Muhammad gave him the title *Sayf Allah* ("Sword of God"). He led the Ridda wars against rebel tribes in Arabia in 632–633, then the initial campaigns in Sasanian Iraq. Reassigned to Syria, he won decisive victories over the Byzantines at [[Damascus]] (634–635) and Yarmouk (636), and the Muslims conquered most of Syria. Umar later demoted him from high command, but he remained a key lieutenant in the sieges of [[Aleppo]] and Homs. Historians regard him as one of the most accomplished generals in Islamic history, though accounts differ on his execution of Malik ibn Nuwayra.

Uzbek monarchy in [[Central Asia]], 1501–1785. It was founded by the Shaybanid dynasty, which claimed descent from [[Genghis Khan]] through [[Jochi]]. Its founder, Muhammad Shaybani, conquered Balkh, Bukhara, [[Samarkand]] and Tashkent, and Abdullah Khan II made Bukhara the permanent capital by 1562. Shaybani's rival [[Babur]], a Timurid prince, was defeated at the Battle of Sar-i Pul in 1501 and turned his ambitions toward India. The Janid dynasty, the last Chinggisid rulers of Bukhara, held power in the 17th and 18th centuries until [[Nader Shah]] of Iran conquered the khanate in 1740. In 1785 the Manghit dynasty formalized its rule, and the state became the Emirate of Bukhara.

Tatar state on the Middle [[Volga]], from the mid-15th century until 1552. One of the successor states of the [[Golden Horde]], it had its capital at [[Kazan]] and covered present-day Tatarstan and neighboring regions. Historians date its founding to 1437 or 1438, when Ulugh Muhammad took power. From 1487 to 1521 it was in effect a Muscovite protectorate, and frequent changes of khan reflected rivalry between pro-Moscow and pro-Crimean nobles. [[Sunni Islam]] was the state religion, and the khanate's towns traded with Russia, Central Asia and the [[Caucasus]]. The [[Tsardom of Russia]] conquered Kazan in 1552 after a siege, and resistance continued until 1557.

Second-largest city in [[Ukraine]], in the northeast of the country. Founded in 1654 as a Cossack fortress, it grew into a major commercial and industrial center within the [[Russian Empire]]. From December 1919 to January 1934 it was the capital of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Machinery, [[Electronics]] and military hardware were its leading industries, and it was a focus of battles in [[World War II]]. Before the 2022 Russian invasion its estimated population was 1,421,125. Russian forces reached its outskirts but were forced back, and by February 2026 four years of shelling and missile attacks had reportedly destroyed a quarter of the city.

Capital and largest city of [[Sudan]], at the confluence of the [[White Nile]] and [[Blue Nile]]. The city was founded in 1821 by Muhammad Ali Pasha, and with the neighboring cities of [[Omdurman]] and Khartoum North it forms a metropolitan area. Mahdist forces captured Khartoum in 1884 after a siege and massacred its Anglo-Egyptian garrison, and British forces reoccupied it in 1898. It became the capital of an independent Sudan in 1956. Between 2023 and 2025 the city saw extensive combat between the armed forces and the Rapid Support Forces. In 2025 the armed forces recaptured it, leaving widespread destruction.

Semi-nomadic Turkic people who built a major commercial empire on the [[Eurasian Steppe]]. For about three centuries (c. 650–965) the Khazars dominated the area from the Volga-Don steppes to the eastern [[Crimea]] and the northern [[Caucasus]]. Their trade linked [[China]], West Asia and [[Kievan Rus']], and the empire commanded the western marches of the [[Silk Road]]. The Khazars were a confederation of Turkic-speaking peoples, and their origins are uncertain because no records survive in their language. The ruling elite reportedly converted to Rabbinic [[Judaism]], probably in the 8th century, though the extent of conversion among the population is unclear. A late 19th-century theory, the Khazar myth, holds that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Khazars, but linguistic and genetic studies have not supported it.

Empire in mainland [[Southeast Asia]], centered on hydraulic cities in what is now northern [[Cambodia]], lasting from 802 to 1431. Its ruler Jayavarman II declared himself chakravartin, or universal ruler, in 802 and went on to rule or dominate most of mainland Southeast Asia. The capital Angkor contains monuments such as [[Angkor Wat]], a Hindu temple dedicated to [[Vishnu]], and the Bayon, built by [[Jayavarman VII]] to honor [[Mahayana]] Buddhism. Satellite imaging shows that Angkor's water management network, at its peak in the 11th to 13th centuries, was the most extensive pre-industrial urban complex in the world. The empire fell to the [[Ayutthaya Kingdom]] in 1431, and scholars continue to debate how far drought and flooding contributed to its decline.

Name given to members of the Communist Party of Kampuchea, which ruled [[Cambodia]] as Democratic Kampuchea from 1975 to 1979. Led by [[Pol Pot]], the group forcibly evacuated the cities and imposed collectivized agriculture. Its policies and purges caused the deaths of 1.5 to 2 million people, around 25% of Cambodia's population, in what is known as the [[Cambodian genocide]]. The regime received at least 90% of its foreign aid from China. Vietnam invaded in 1979 and removed the regime, which fled to [[Thailand]]. In 2014 two leaders, Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan, were jailed for life for crimes against humanity.

[[Austroasiatic languages|Austroasiatic]] language and the official language of [[Cambodia]]. Spoken by some 13 million people in Cambodia, it is also used by Khmer communities in [[Thailand]] and [[Vietnam]]. Most speakers use Central Khmer, though the speech of [[Phnom Penh]] is considered a separate dialect. Khmer is an analytic, isolating language with no inflections, and its word order is subject–verb–object. Unlike neighboring Burmese, Thai, Lao and Vietnamese, it is not tonal. Its vocabulary has been considerably influenced by [[Sanskrit]] and [[Pali]], especially in royal and religious registers. It has been written in the Khmer script, an abugida descended from the Brahmi script, since at least the 7th century.

Group of African languages known for click consonants, once classified as one family. Joseph Greenberg proposed the grouping, but linguists now reject its genetic unity and treat Khoisan as a *sprachbund*, a set of languages that share features through contact. It is now held to comprise three distinct families and two language isolates, spoken mainly in the [[Kalahari Desert]] of [[Namibia]] and [[Botswana]] and in central [[Tanzania]]. Clicks are phonemes, and the Juǀʼhoan language has 48 click consonants. Khoekhoe, with about a quarter of a million speakers, is the most widespread. Most Khoisan languages are endangered, and many have no written record.

Historical region of the [[Iranian plateau]] in West and Central Asia. In its strict historical sense it covered most of present-day [[Afghanistan]] and northeastern [[Iran]], extending to the [[Amu Darya]] river, but the name was often used loosely for a larger region that included much of Transoxiana. The name, Persian in origin, is often glossed as "the Eastern Province." The [[Sasanian Empire]] first made Khorasan an administrative division in the 6th century, during the reign of Kavad I or [[Khosrow I]]. Early Islamic usage applied the name to much of the territory east of Jibal, or Iraq Ajami. Nishapur, Merv, [[Herat]] and Balkh were its four principal cities.

[[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] king of kings of Iran, 531–579, also known as Anushirvan. In 532 he signed the Perpetual Peace with the Byzantine emperor [[Justinian I]], who paid 11,000 pounds of gold. Khosrow broke the treaty in 540, sacked [[Antioch]] and deported its population to Persia. In alliance with the [[Göktürks]], he ended the Hephthalite Empire, and Iranian forces conquered [[Yemen]]. He carried out major social, military and economic reforms, including a professional army and new cities, and he promoted literature and philosophy. At his death the Sasanian Empire was at its greatest extent since Shapur II, from Yemen to Gandhara. He was succeeded by his son Hormizd IV.

Persianate Sunni Muslim empire of Turkic mamluk origin, 1077–1231. Ruled by the Anushtegin dynasty, it began as vassals of the [[Seljuk Empire]] and became independent around 1190. It grew into the most powerful state in and around Persia, taking territory from the Ghurid Empire and threatening the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. At its height it covered an estimated 2.3 to 3.6 million sq km, and its army was made up largely of Kipchak Turks. In 1219 the Mongols under [[Genghis Khan]] invaded and conquered most of the empire within two years. A rump state survived in western Iran until 1231, when it was conquered after the death of Jalal al-Din Mangburni, the last Khwarazmshah.

Province of [[Pakistan]] in the northwest, bordering [[Afghanistan]] to the west. It is the fourth-largest Pakistani province by land area and the third by population. The area was the site of ancient Gandhara and a stronghold of [[Buddhism]] before [[Islam]] became dominant after the 11th-century conquest of the Hindu Shahi kingdom by the Ghaznavids. The province was created in 1901 under the [[British Raj]] as the North-West Frontier Province, and it took its present name in 2010. Its capital is [[Peshawar]].

Type of intentional community in [[Israel]]. The first kibbutz, Degania, was founded in 1910. Kibbutzim began as utopian communities combining [[Socialism|socialism]] and [[Zionism]], and they were traditionally based on [[Agriculture|agriculture]]. In 2010 there were 270 kibbutzim with a total population of 126,000, whose factories and farms produced 9% of Israel's industrial output and 40% of its agricultural output. Some kibbutzim have also developed substantial high-tech and military industries, and in recent decades some have been privatized.
